newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to require more energy-efficient refrigerators.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to require more energy-efficient refrigerators.

text.p: Ending a two-year standoff between green groups and appliance makers, the Clinton administration is set to require 30 percent more energy savings from refrigerators, industry and environmental officials said Tuesday.

The tighter standards, to be announced by Energy Secretary Federico Pena on Wednesday, would go into effect in July 2001, one year later than environmental groups had sought but two years earlier than manufacturers wanted.

"We see this (rule) eventually providing energy savings equal to the power output of about eight large power plants," said Edward Osann, senior associate with the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.
He said the new refrigerators would conserve about 25 billion kilowatt hours of electricity annually by 2020.

Consumers could end up paying $160 more for refrigerators if manufacturers pass on the higher costs of making the new models, but appliance makers said the price might not climb much above today's average of $600.

"The combination of a competitive environment within the industry and with mega-retailers, and the fact that we have been able to achieve trememdous productivity improvements in the manufacturing process, mean consumers have not been forced to pay more," said Charles Samuels, lobbyist for the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers.

According to the group, it would cost about $70 more per refrigerator to build the new models, and the Energy Department estimated that increase could be more than doubled between manufacturers and retailers.
"Even if that were in fact the initial up front additional cost, ... it will be paid back in less than five years, just in energy bill savings to consumers," said Osann.

Energy conservation groups and manufacturers have battled over raising refrigerator energy efficiency ever since an agreement on new standards fell apart two years ago with the ascent of an anti-regulatory Republican majority in Congress.
Appliance manufacturers walked away from the agreement in 1995 and persuaded lawmakers to block the Energy Department from issuing the rule for a year.
The two sides were able to reach a compromise this year because of recent developments in refrigerator insulating foam materials.

Big appliance makers, with the notable exception of Whirlpool Corp., had complained they needed more lead time to meet the energy savings goal while also complying with clean air rules that called for eliminating the use of ozone-depleting hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFC).

General Electric, Maytag Corp., Raytheon Co.'s Amana, and AB Electrolux's Frigidaire pressed for the tighter requirement to come into effect only in 2003, when they were scheduled to stop using HCFC's.

The 1994 proposal had included a two-tier standard that would have settled for a 23 percent increase in energy savings for refrigerators that were using HCFC substitutes, which consumed more energy than HCFC.

But over the last two years, researchers have found a new material that is as energy-efficient as HCFC and can be used instead of HCFC for insulating refrigerators. Chemical manufacturer AlliedSignal Inc. has said it would be able to supply enough of the HCFC substitute by 2000.
